tldr: We proposed a reinforcement learning framework that safely catches human-thrown unseen objects in real time using a humanoid dexterous hand, relying solely on a single egocentric camera (head-mounted camera). By training only on primitive shapes in simulation, we demonstrated high catching accuracy across 9 types of unseen objects, including plush toys and chip bags, via zero-shot sim-to-real transfer.
hero_caption: Sequential frames of real-world underhand and overhand catching motions. The robot dynamically moves its hand forward and backward to match the object's flight trajectory and distance, intercepting and wrapping its fingers around objects such as a Takis bag, a plush turtle, a strawberry toy, and a sandbag.
overview:
Dynamic manipulation to catch incoming projectiles is an extremely difficult task that requires visual perception and motor control to coordinate within milliseconds. Prior research on robotic catching was often limited to low-rebound sandbags or known spheres, or relied heavily on high-precision external motion capture, creating significant barriers to real-world generalization. For humanoid robots in particular, wrist torque limits are remarkably low—around $5\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$—meaning aggressive movements constantly risk exceeding actuator hardware limits and breaking the robot.

To address this, the authors developed "Catch It All!", a framework that uses only a single egocentric RGB-D camera to safely catch objects with unseen shapes, elasticities, and deformabilities. The approach has three core elements. First, a smooth grasp reward based on fingertip-to-surface distance was designed to learn multi-finger grasps that rapidly adapt to diverse objects. Second, a curriculum learning strategy over torque clipping and penalties was introduced, enabling exploration while strictly respecting actuator limits. Third, a teacher policy trained with full state access was distilled (via DAgger) into a student policy operating purely on noisy visual history.

In experiments, after training in IsaacGym, robustness was evaluated via sim-to-sim transfer in MuJoCo, followed by zero-shot deployment onto a physical Unitree G1 humanoid. Despite seeing only primitive geometric shapes during training, the policy achieved a 38.9% success rate for underhand catches and 36.1% for overhand catches across 9 types of unseen real-world thrown objects (including plushes, snack bags, and elastic toys). This vividly demonstrates that the method achieves high generalization while maintaining safety in dynamic tasks where collecting teleoperation data is virtually impossible.
contributions: Built a reinforcement learning framework capable of underhand and overhand catching of unseen objects using only a single egocentric camera, without external sensors or prior demonstrations.

Achieved adaptive multi-finger grasps for objects with diverse shapes, elasticities, and deformabilities through a grasp reward based on maximum fingertip-to-surface distance paired with a throw curriculum.

Enabled safe, high-frequency execution near hardware limits on a compliant humanoid with wrist torque limits as low as $5\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$, using a curriculum that progressively adjusts torque clipping limits and penalties.
Demonstrated zero-shot transfer from simulation training (IsaacGym) to a physical Unitree G1 robot, achieving high catching success rates across 9 real-world objects unseen during training.

sections.heading: Why is it so hard for a humanoid to catch a flying object?
sections.summary: Dynamic catching demands low-latency, compliant visuomotor reflexes on the millisecond scale. Compared to industrial arms, humanoids feature lower joint torque limits and control bandwidths, making it exceptionally hard to acquire high-frequency reactive motions without damaging hardware.
sections.details:
Catching a projectile mid-air is a challenging dynamic manipulation problem that requires tightly coupled synchronization between visual perception and motor control. Flying objects vary widely in geometry, mass, and impact rebound (elasticity), demanding low-latency visuomotor reflexes that adapt on the fly.

For humanoids, this challenge is even steeper. Unlike quadrupeds or rigid industrial manipulators, humanoids prioritize lightweight designs and energy efficiency, resulting in joint torque limits as low as $5\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$ at the wrists. Aggressive catching motions can easily exceed these actuator limits and cause mechanical failure.

Prior works simplified the problem by restricting catches to low-rebound, easy-to-grasp sandbags, relying on external high-precision motion capture, or limiting setups to short handovers between two arms. While some studies demonstrated catching diverse objects in simulation, zero-shot transfer to a diverse set of real-world unseen objects remained unsolved.

This paper proposes "Catch It All!", a system that catches unseen projectiles underhand and overhand using only a single egocentric camera (head camera), without human demonstrations or motion capture. The key to generalizing across unseen objects while operating safely within hardware limits lies in careful reward design and safety curricula.

sections.heading: The constraints that held back prior catching research
sections.summary: Conventional catching research made the task tractable by fitting trajectory models to known objects, using external motion capture, or restricting objects to sandbags and spheres. Consequently, generalizing to unseen objects under egocentric vision remained out of reach.
sections.details:
Robotic catching involves two major technical hurdles.

### II-A Difficulties of Dynamic Adaptation in Catching
Projectiles spend only a fraction of a second in the air. Within that window, the robot must estimate the object's state, predict its trajectory, and plan and execute full-body or arm trajectories. Under egocentric vision from a head camera, aggressive robot movements can cause the object to exit the field of view or introduce significant observation noise. Furthermore, projectile spin alters aerodynamic trajectories, while the center of mass and moments of inertia remain unknown until impact, frequently causing the robot to close its fingers too abruptly and swat the object away.

### II-B Limitations in Generalization
Prior works imposed several constraints to overcome these challenges:
- **Object restrictions**: Most approaches were restricted to low-rebound objects like sandbags or simple spheres.
- **Sensor restrictions**: Rather than using onboard cameras, setups relied on expensive optical motion capture systems covering the room to track precise 3D object positions.
- **Embodiment restrictions**: To reduce degrees of freedom, setups mounted nets onto quadrupeds or pinched projectiles between front legs instead of using multi-finger hands.

Moreover, humanoids possess lower motor control bandwidths and torque limits than industrial arms, quickly hitting actuator limits under violent, high-frequency reactive motions. This work removes all these constraints, tackling the most challenging setting: egocentric vision, unseen objects, a dexterous hand, and a humanoid platform.

sections.heading: A learning architecture that wraps around unseen objects and protects hardware
sections.summary: Using a humanoid equipped with a high-DOF 20-DOF hand, the framework adopts teacher-student training. Safe and robust catching is learned through a fingertip-to-surface distance reward using spherical approximation alongside three progressive curricula for torque limits and penalties.
sections.details:
### III-A System Architecture
A seated Unitree G1 EDU serves as the experimental platform. An egocentric stereo camera (ZED2i) is mounted on the head. At the end of the arm is a 20-DOF House of Dextra hand. This hand matches the weight of a 16-DOF LEAP hand (approx. 600g) while adding an extra finger (5 fingers in total), enabling diverse grasps tailored to object geometry. To stay within the G1's arm payload (nominal 3kg), the palm was custom-fabricated from lightweight hollow carbon fiber.

### III-B Policy Learning
The task is formulated as a Partially Observable Markov Decision Process (POMDP). Observations include proprioception (joint angles and velocities), 3D object position extracted in real time via SAM2-Tiny, and 3D bounding box dimensions. The arm is controlled via 6D relative pose commands through inverse kinematics (IK), while the hand is driven by absolute joint position control.

Because real-world camera observations suffer from stereo depth noise and frequent occlusions outside the field of view, direct RL exploration from scratch is difficult. A two-stage teacher-student framework (Fig. F2) is adopted instead:
- **Stage 1 (Teacher)**: Separate underhand and overhand teacher policies are trained using PPO in IsaacGym with access to ground-truth object states.
- **Stage 2 (Student)**: The frozen teacher's actions are distilled via DAgger into a student policy conditioned on noisy observations and a 50-step (1-second) observation history.

To accelerate training, only primitive geometries (7 basic shapes like cuboids and spheres) are used in simulation, while friction, mass, scale, restitution, and latency are heavily domain-randomized.

### III-C Reward Design: Fingertip-to-Surface Distance Reward
To wrap around incoming objects securely without swatting them away, a reward based on the distance from fingertips to the object surface was designed. Because exact mesh-to-mesh distance queries are computationally expensive in simulation, the object is approximated by its bounding sphere radius $r_{\mathrm{obj}}$. An exponential reward is computed as $\exp(-10(\max_{\mathrm{ftip}}\|p_* - p_{\mathrm{obj}}\| - r_{\mathrm{obj}}))$, increasing as the maximum distance between any fingertip and the surface shrinks. This yields a dense reward signal that guides the fingers to smoothly conform to the object, even when irregular shapes prevent all fingers from making contact simultaneously.

### III-D Three Curricula
- **Throw Target Curriculum (Overhand only)**: Because overhand catches are hard to explore initially, throws start directly 10cm above and 10cm behind the hand's rest pose, gradually expanding to a wider throwing range.
- **Torque Clip Curriculum**: Designed to protect the G1's strict wrist torque limits (as low as $5\,\mathrm{N\cdot m}$). Clipping strictly at the nominal limits early on inhibits exploration. The policy initially explores under nominal clipping limits, and the clipping window is expanded up to $2\times$ nominal limits as learning progresses. Applying a penalty to torques exceeding nominal limits encourages the policy to confidently utilize the hardware limits while converging to safe torque profiles.
- **Penalty Curriculum**: Regularization weights on joint velocities, accelerations, and torques are scaled from $1\times$ at the start up to $20\times$ near the end of training, steering the policy toward smooth, hardware-safe behavior.

sections.heading: Catching unseen chip bags without bouncing: zero-shot transfer in action
sections.summary: Experiments were conducted in simulation (IsaacGym), across simulators via Sim-to-Sim (MuJoCo), and on the physical G1 humanoid. The proposed framework demonstrated strong generalization across novel shapes, elasticities, and deformabilities, substantially outperforming baselines in catching success and hardware safety.
sections.details:
### IV-A Simulation and Sim-to-Sim Evaluation
Policies trained in IsaacGym were evaluated both inside IsaacGym (32,768 episodes) and in MuJoCo (1,280 episodes) across contact physics engines. Evaluated objects totaled 20: 7 training primitives, 7 unseen irregular objects, and 6 elongated objects (Fig. F4).

- **Generalization**: On unseen irregular shapes, the student policy experienced only a ~5% drop in success rate compared to training primitives. Variations in restitution (bounciness) caused minimal performance degradation. However, for tumbling elongated objects, performance dropped by ~20% because the policy does not observe the object's rotational velocity.
- **Baseline Comparisons**: An MPC baseline and an end-to-end RL baseline trained directly on noisy visual observations achieved near-0% success rates. An RL model trained without the torque clip curriculum scored well in IsaacGym but degraded sharply in MuJoCo Sim-to-Sim transfer.
- **Safety Verification**: Comparing mechanical power across joints showed that the proposed curriculum operated at significantly lower mechanical power than the uncurriculated baseline, confirming catches are executed without overloading wrist joints or motors.
- **Grasp Reward Ablation**: Compared against contact-duration stability rewards and contact-sensor-based rewards from prior literature, the proposed fingertip-to-surface distance reward achieved the highest success rates in both Sim and Sim-to-Sim. Contact-based rewards overfit to binary contact events, making them vulnerable to contact discrepancies across physics engines.

### IV-B Real-World Zero-Shot Catching
The student policy was deployed zero-shot onto the Unitree G1 to catch 9 human-thrown unseen objects (Fig. F6):
- **Plushes (Low rebound)**: Panda, turtle, sandbag
- **Deformable (Snack bags, etc.)**: Takis bag, strawberry, pineapple
- **Rigid & Elastic**: Plastic bowl, ellipsoid toy, rigid bear toy

Throws were split across short (1.0–1.4m), medium (1.4–1.8m), and long (>1.8m) distances. Despite including deformable and highly elastic objects that cannot be modeled in rigid-body simulators, the policy achieved an overall success rate of 38.9% for underhand catches and 36.1% for overhand catches (Table III). As shown in Fig. F9, the fingers adaptively wrap around the contours of the incoming objects to secure a firm hold.

In a comparison test where an expert human teleoperated the robot at 15Hz, only 3 out of 44 catches succeeded (6.8% success rate). In dynamic tasks where communication and human reaction delays are fatal, the onboard closed-loop RL policy demonstrates clear superiority.

sections.heading: Summary and future outlook: toward ultimate whole-body dynamic catching
sections.summary: We demonstrated a framework that safely and adaptively catches unseen objects on a humanoid equipped with a single egocentric camera and a dexterous hand. Future work aims to expand the workspace by incorporating whole-body coordination with the lower body.
sections.details:
"Catch It All!" realizes dynamic manipulation capable of catching diverse unseen projectiles using only a single head-mounted egocentric camera, without human demonstrations or external motion capture. It reveals that on a humanoid with sensitive torque limits, combining a torque clip curriculum with a distance-based grasp reward is essential for achieving both dynamic agility and hardware safety.

Current limitations include controlling only the seated upper body (arm and hand) without extending to whole-body control. The authors plan to extend this framework to full-body coordination including leg stepping, significantly expanding the catching workspace to intercept projectiles thrown further away and enhancing impact absorption upon catch.

takeaways: Contact rewards based on discrete ON/OFF contact states struggle with sim-to-sim discrepancies; a smooth fingertip-to-surface distance reward using spherical approximation provides significantly better sim-to-real transfer and generalization.

When learning dynamic actions on robots with tight torque limits, strict early clipping hinders exploration. A curriculum that starts at nominal limits, gradually widens the clip window, and penalizes excess torque enables safe exploration near limits.
For dynamic projectile interception tasks where latency renders teleoperation data collection virtually impossible, fast simulation RL combined with distillation is exceptionally practical.
limitations: The robot is constrained to a seated position and does not support whole-body control (such as stepping or torso translation) to cover a larger workspace.
Because visual observations are limited to 3D position and bounding box dimensions, catching performance drops by about 20% on tumbling, elongated objects (e.g., hammers or sticks).
The overall real-world success rate remains in the upper 30% range, leaving a notable failure rate compared to human catching capabilities or static manipulation tasks.
